content: Corticosteroids, including ACTH, have been utilized in the treatment of childhood epilepsy, excluding epileptic spasms. However, their effectiveness in controlling seizures, improving cognitive function, and enhancing quality of life, as well as their tolerability, remain unclear. These medications are also associated with significant adverse effects. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of corticosteroids in terms of seizure control, cognitive improvements, quality of life, and tolerability when compared to placebo or other antiepileptic drugs in children with epilepsy, excluding those with epileptic spasms. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, DARE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The search was completed as of August 1, 2014. Reference lists of retrieved studies were also reviewed to identify additional relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children under the age of 16 with epilepsy who were treated with corticosteroids. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion and extracted data. The outcomes assessed included seizure cessation, reduction in seizure frequency, cognitive improvements, quality of life, and adverse effects of corticosteroids. Only one RCT met the inclusion criteria. This study involved five children in a double-blind, cross-over design. However, one child was withdrawn prematurely, and another was excluded due to having infantile spasms, leaving three children for analysis. The study investigated the effects of adrenocorticotrophin hormone (ACTH 4-9). Among the three children analyzed, one experienced a 25% to 50% reduction in seizures at both low and high doses of corticosteroids compared to placebo. Another child showed a reduction in seizures only at the higher dose, while the third child did not experience any reduction in seizures at either dose. No adverse effects were reported in this study. The authors concluded that since the last version of this review, no new evidence has emerged to support the efficacy of corticosteroids in treating childhood epilepsies, excluding epileptic spasms. Clinicians should carefully consider this lack of evidence when deciding to use corticosteroids in the management of childhood epilepsy outside the context of epileptic spasms.
